newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban square up to Afghan warlord, world opinion.
newsitem.headline: Taleban square up to Afghan warlord, world opinion.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban militia, fresh from a victorious sweep across three-quarters of Afghanistan, were squaring up on Tuesday to a powerful northern warlord as well as attempts by the world community to influence events.

Taleban forces came into direct confrontation with General Abdul Rashid Dostum's organised army for the first time on Monday after capturing Jabal os-Siraj, a stonghold of former government military chief Ahmed Shah Masood, 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul, and pushing on towards the Salang Tunnel.
Dostum had previously managed to stay away from the fighting between Taleban and the former Kabul government, which he also opposed.

But Dostum responded to the Taleban advance by moving tanks and artillery several km (miles) south of the strategic tunnel that links Kabul with north and central Asia, blocking further progress by the Islamic militants.
A Taleban commander at the Salang front, Mullah Ghulam Mohammad, told a visiting United Nations official in the presence of reporters that Dostum appeared bent on confrontation.
Officials with Dostum's well-armed Jumbish-i-Milli faction had earlier said they were ready to fight if the Taleban pushed further north.
"We don't want to join this war," said a senior Jumbish official who declined to be named. "But if they (the Taleban) attack, we would defend ourselves."

Other Taleban forces turned east from Jabal os-Siraj, capturing the town of Golbahar, 10 km (six miles) away at the foot of the Panjsher valley, homeland of Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik forces and scene of his guerrilla exploits against Soviet occupation forces in the 1980s.

Aid workers at Jabal os-Siraj said the town as well as Charikar and Golbahar had been calm overnight but they had no information on whether there had been any fighting on frontlines north and east Jabal.
Meanwhile, United Nations' special envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl said he was trying to arrange peace talks among the country's warring factions.
He told German radio he would visit two more groups after his meeting with the dominant Taleban Islamic militia, which took the capital Kabul on Friday.
Afghanistan's ousted government has refused to give up office and called on the United Nations to probe Pakistani support for the Taleban.

"We earnestly expect the United Nations to immediately send a fact-finding mission into Afghanistan (to) assess the level and degree of cross-border intervention here," said deputy foreign minister, Abdul Rahim Ghafoorzai.

Pakistan, which has denied accusations by the former government led by President Burhanuddin Rabbani that it supports the Taleban, sent a diplomat to Kabul this week to reopen the Pakistani embassy here.
The United States toughened its line towards the Taleban on Monday, condemning their execution of former president Najibullah and stressing concerns over such issues as terrorism and narcotics.
"The situation on the ground is quite murky," spokesman Nicholas Burns said. He also said there was no thought being given to upgrading diplomatic ties with Afghanistan.
The United States has not had an embassy in Kabul since 1989 due to civil war and there has not been a U.S. ambassador in the country since 1979 when a former envoy was assassinated.

In Paris, Federico Mayor, Director General of the United Nations Educational Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), said he was disturbed by reports that women were being denied equal rights to education and work since the Taleban took over Kabul last week.

"While respecting the rights of the Afghan people to freely chose their government, I want to remind their new leaders of the importance of creating an atmosphere in which tolerance of different ethnic, gender and political groups can prevail," Mayor said.

Decisions on many issues, including the sensitive question of whether women will be allowed to work, and whether girls will be allowed to go to school, have been referred to the Taleban's Kandahar-based supreme council led by Mullah Mohammad Omar, who founded the movement in 1994.
